transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-18 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~45 mins | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Martinez (AE, Redwood); Samir Khan (SE, Redwood); Priya Rao (Product, Redwood); Jordan Lee (CTO, Atlas); Maya Patel (ML Engineer, Atlas); Chris Nguyen (Infra, Atlas); Lina Ortiz (PM, Atlas)

00:00 Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a quick walkthrough of Redwood Optimize focused on batching and the KV/prefix cache, and then get into cost models and a proposed POC.
00:12 Jordan: Sounds good, we only have 45 minutes so keen to see the numbers.
00:18 Samir: Quick agenda — 1) latency & batching basics, 2) cache strategies (prefix vs KV), 3) cost model examples with Atlas-like traffic, 4) questions & next steps.
00:30 Maya: Quick note on our side — we do a lot of short queries, average prompt length 30 tokens, responses 60 tokens, bursty qps around 200, baseline 99th latency target 300ms.
00:45 Samir: That helps. With short prompt/response patterns we often recommend prefix caching first — if you have repeated prefixes or system prompts, that gives huge token savings — then KV cache for session state / long-form context.
01:00 Alex: I'll surface some high level numbers: on a sample workload like yours, enabling prefix cache can reduce token generation by 20-40% for templated prompts; KV cache can cut repeated decoding cost by another 10-30% depending on session reuse.
01:12 Jordan: When you say KV cache, is that the same as the Redwood "KV cache" we saw in the doc? How persistent is it, and what's the eviction policy?
01:22 Samir: Good q. Our KV cache stores key-value pairs from the attention cache between calls for the same session. It's memory-resident on the serving node and we expose TTLs and evict-by-LRU policies; for Dedicated you can choose larger capacity and pin sessions. In hosted we do sharded cache with automatic eviction when memory pressure increases.
01:45 Chris: Sharded — does that mean keys could be on different nodes and we could see a miss if the request lands somewhere else?
01:52 Samir: By default we route sticky to the same pool for session affinity, but we also have a KV-sync mode for cross-node lookups at slightly higher latency; for 99th SLOs we usually recommend session-affinity + hot-sharding.
02:10 Maya: And how about prefix cache? Is that stored separately?
02:14 Samir: Prefix caching stores encoded prefix tokens (embeddings/kv) so that the model doesn't re-run the prefix repeatedly. It's much smaller footprint and can be shared across requests; eviction is more conservative.
02:24 Lina: We have strict PII rules — if we cache customer data, we need encryption and easy purge.
02:29 Alex: Right; we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for encrypting cached material at rest, and purge APIs to delete cached prefixes/kv for compliance. We'll include the security one-pager.
02:40 Jordan: Performance numbers — can you show expected latency and cost delta for our traffic if we enable both optimizations?
02:47 Samir: I pulled a quick model. Baseline hosted run (no cache, small batch sizes): avg per-call token cost X, per-token latency Y. With continuous batching optimized for your qps (target batch size 8–16) and prefix+KV caching enabled we estimate ~35% token reduction and 20–30% CPU/GPU utilization reduction, translating to roughly 25–40% cost savings depending on model variant and quantization.
03:10 Maya: Is that across all models or specific to the 13B family?
03:14 Samir: Tied to model and quantization. For a 13B fp16 model you see smaller absolute savings vs a 70B where prefix amortization is greater. The spreadsheet I'll share has per-model rows.
03:26 Chris: What's the impact on tail latency when you enable prefix cache and batching? We worry about P95/P99 spikes during bursts.
03:32 Samir: Good concern. Batching helps throughput but can increase queueing latency for single requests; we mitigate with latency-aware routing, max-wait timers, and pre-emptive small-batch fast-paths. The prefix cache usually reduces decode time so P99 often improves if the cache hit rate is high. In our tests with similar burstiness, enabling cache + adaptive batching kept P99 under your 300ms target in 90% of runs; we'll schedule a bench to validate with your traffic.
03:55 Alex: Also worth noting fallbacks — if cache misses spike, we automatically failover to a lower-cost model variant or route to a dedicated pool if you have a reserved capacity plan.
04:05 Jordan: Can you run this on our VPC/private deployment? We prefer private for data residency.
04:10 Priya: Yes — our Private offering supports the same Optimize tooling; KV/prefix cache runs in-customer VPC, and you can configure where the cache persists. We support on-prem pinning and additional audit logs.
04:22 Lina: On audit logs — do you capture token-level traces? We need to show which prompts were served and when for compliance.
04:28 Priya: We provide token-level cost breakdowns with redaction options; logs can be exported to your SIEM. We'll share the audit docs.
04:36 Maya: A practical question on tuning — what batch sizes should we use? Our qps is bursty, sometimes hitting 200 for short windows.
04:42 Samir: For bursty workloads we recommend dynamic batching with a target average batch of 8–16, max batch 32. If your median qps is lower, we can set a shorter max-wait to cap latency. For example, at 200 qps with avg tokens 90, batches of 12–16 kept GPU utilization high and latency acceptable in our Atlas-like simulations.
05:04 Jordan: How much engineering time is needed to instrument and enable prefix caching?
05:08 Alex: Minimal — you need to tag the templates/prompts you want cached and add a short config flag in the API call. Samir: we'll give a config example and a migration checklist; most customers onboard in 1–2 sprints.
05:20 Chris: Any limitations on which prefixes can be cached — like dynamic user data?
05:25 Samir: We recommend caching only stable system prompts and shared prefixes; user-specific PII should not be cached unless encrypted and explicitly allowed. The SDK supports per-call cache_control flags.
05:36 Maya: On the cost model, can you walk through a concrete example with numbers?
05:40 Samir: Sure. Example simplified: baseline cost per 1k requests = $A (no cache), avg tokens generated per request 90 => tokens per 1k = 90k. With prefix cache hit rate 40% and KV hit 20% additional, token generation drops to ~58k per 1k requests. If model pricing is $0.03 per 1k tokens, that's $1.74 vs $2.70 — ~35% savings. Add batching gains reducing GPU instance hours by 25% — total infra+token savings ~30-40%. We'll send the exact spreadsheet with your qps and token lengths.
06:14 Jordan: How accurate are these estimates — what's variance?
06:17 Samir: Variance depends on hit rates and traffic shape; we provide pessimistic/expected/optimistic scenarios in the sheet. Typical +/- 10–15% from predicted if traffic assumptions hold.
06:28 Lina: Security again — encryption at rest for cached items using our KMS: yes?
06:33 Alex: Yes, customer-managed keys supported for Private and Dedicated; hosted supports envelope encryption and we can discuss SOC2 controls.
06:40 Maya: On the POC, do you require dedicated capacity?
06:44 Samir: Not necessarily — we can run a hosted POC with a reserved burst pool for the benchmark window. If you want fully isolated testing, Dedicated POC is possible but takes longer to provision.
06:56 Jordan: What does the POC entail?
07:00 Alex: Quick plan — 1) share config & test dataset, 2) Redwood runs a 2-hour benchmark simulating your traffic, 3) we collect P50/P95/P99 latencies, token counts, cache hit rates, and cost metrics, 4) review and tune config.
07:13 Maya: Does Redwood require us to share real user data for the bench?
07:17 Samir: You can sanitize or use replayed synthetic traffic; we often do a hashed/anonymized sample to get realistic token shapes without PII.
07:24 Chris: Operational question — if we see a cache inconsistency after a deploy, what are rollback steps?
07:29 Priya: We have cache invalidation APIs and rollouts can be canaryed per shard; we recommend a two-step deploy: config behind feature flag + monitor cache hit metrics. If problem, flip the flag and purge keys.
07:44 Jordan: Pricing asks — Can you give ballpark committed pricing for Dedicated if we want reserved pool?
07:48 Alex: Ballpark yes, we'll put formal numbers in the sheet. Committed discounts depend on term and capacity; typical savings vs on-demand are 20–40% depending on commit.
07:58 Maya: Any competitors doing a better job here? We looked at OpenAI and Anthropic notes.
08:02 Samir: OpenAI offers managed endpoints but less control over KV/prefix caching; Anthropic has different tradeoffs. Our differentiation is observable Optimize tooling + unified deploy options and per-token breakdowns.
08:15 Lina: Ok next steps recap?
08:18 Alex: Recap — Alex will send pricing & security docs; Samir will share KV sizing spreadsheet and example configs; Atlas will provide sample traffic and confirm POC window. We'll aim to run the POC the week of 2026-03-29.
08:31 Jordan: That works, I'll get Maya and Chris to own sample traffic and infra checks.
08:36 Alex: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
08:40 Meeting end.
